body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Giralda (1894). Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.
Giralda was a steamship built as a private yacht in 1894. In 1898, the government of Spain acquired her.

She subsequently was in commission in the Spanish Navy from 1898 to 1934, seeing service as a dispatch vessel, as the royal yacht of Queen Regent Maria Christina and King Alfonso XIII, as a training ship, and as a hydrographic survey ship.
She spent her final years as a ship of the Spanish Republican Navy after the proclamation of the Second Spanish Republic in 1931.
Design
Giralda was a 1,508-gross register ton steel-hulled steamship rigged as a three-masted schooner. 80 metres (19 ft 0 in).

Giralda had two triple-expansion engines, each with four crankshafts. Her coal bunkers had a capacity of 496 long tons (504 tonnes) and surrounded her machinery, providing it with protection. 1 mph) during sea trials.

Above deck, Giralda had a forecastle, a 50-meter (164-foot) long central house amidships, and a cabin aft that housed her engine room. The central house included a waiting room, a saloon, a dining room, and a smoking room. A gallery to starboard connected these rooms. 90 metres (9 ft 6 in) above the cabin sole.

Forward of the boiler room she had four large cabins, accessed by a staircase leading down from a room in the central house aft of the smoking room. The owner's cabin and adjoining rooms were aft of the engine room and were decorated with mahogany joinery and silk upholstery.
Large skylights and frosted-glass rooflights allowed sunlight into the rooms, and all of the ship's compartments had electric lighting. Her hull was divided into watertight compartments.
Construction

Giralda was constructed by the Fairfield Shipbuilding and Engineering Company at Govan in Glasgow, Scotland, in the United Kingdom for the British statesman and sportsman Hugh McCalmont. She was laid down with the shipyard number 376 and launched on 28 August 1894.
She conducted her sea trials on 5 November 1894, and was registered in Glasgow on 9 November. McCalmont took delivery of her upon her completion in December 1894. Her official number was 104586.
Service history
Private yacht

Following her delivery to McCalmont, Giralda became part of the Royal Yacht Squadron and participated in several regattas. At the time she entered service, she was the fastest private yacht in the world.
She broke the speed record for a crossing from England to the Mediterranean Sea, steaming the 1,000 nautical miles (1,900 km, 1,200 mi) from Dartmouth to Gibraltar in 61 hours.
In 1895 the Japanese government tried to buy Giralda, intending to operate her as a fast despatch vessel in the Imperial Japanese Navy. The sale did not go through.
In early 1898, with war between Spain and the United States imminent, Giralda was offered for sale to the United States government. The United States had no interest in buying her.
She then was offered to the Kingdom of Spain, which purchased her on 28 March 1898 for 60,000 pounds sterling, equivalent at the time to US$300,000 or 2,250,000 Spanish pesetas.
Spanish-American War

Giralda completed her delivery voyage to Spain with her arrival on 27 March 1898 at Barcelona, where she began conversion for naval service as an aviso. Her commanding officer, Capitán de fragata (Frigate Captain) Rafael Rodríguez de Vera, was appointed on 1 April.
After the installation of her armament and loading of coal, she departed Barcelona on 20 April 1898 bound for Cádiz.

The Spanish-American War began on 25 April 1898, when the United States declared war on Spain, stipulating that the declaration was retroactive to 21 April, when it had begun to commit acts of war, such as blockading Cuba and seizing Spanish merchant ships.

The Spanish Navy's 1st Squadron, under Contralmirante (Counter Admiral) Pascual Cervera y Topete, deployed to the Caribbean Sea, where it became trapped at Santiago de Cuba on the southeastern coast of Cuba on 27 May 1898 by the ships of the United States Navy's Flying Squadron, reinforced on 1 June by the ships of the North Atlantic Squadron.

To relieve the pressure on Cervera's squadron, the Spanish Navy began to plan a counterattack by ships of the 2nd Squadron, still in Spanish home waters under the command of Contralmirante (Counter Admiral) Manuel de la Cámara y Livermoore. The plan called for Giralda to operate as part of the 2nd Squadron's 1st Division.

Under Cámara's direct command, the 1st Division, which also included the armored cruiser Emperador Carlos V and the auxiliary cruisers Meteoro, Patriota, and Rapido, was to make a transatlantic voyage to Bermuda, where it would receive further instructions.

It then was to steam northward along the United States East Coast, pausing to bombard an American city along the way, to Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada. After receiving additiional instructions there, the division was to steam to the Turks and Caicos Islands for operations in the Caribbean.

In the end, these plans were cancelled, and Giralda did not take part in an abortive attempt by Cámara's squadron to steam to the Philippines in June-July 1898. Giralda thus remained in Spanish home waters throughout the war, seeing no combat.

The Spanish Navy suffered heavy losses during the war, which ended in August 1898 and resulted in the Spanish Empire losing the Philippines and Guam in the Spanish East Indies and Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Caribbean.
Repatriation of Columbus's remains
In the Spanish-American War's aftermath, the unprotected cruiser Conde de Venadito departed Cuba carrying the remains of Christopher Columbus.

She arrived at Cádiz at approximately 10:20 on 16 January 1899 and immediately transferred Columbus's casket and verification paperwork to Giralda, a transfer managed by Cristóbal Colón, 14th Duke of Veragua, Columbus's direct descendant, who delayed all public ceremony for the transfer until the arrival of the remains at Seville.

Giralda then steamed along the coast of Spain to Sanlúcar de Barrameda and from there up the Guadalquivir River to Seville, which she reached on 19 January 1899. As she arrived, she received a grand salute by the sirens of ships on the scene.
In a public ceremony, Columbus's remains were brought ashore and transported to Seville Cathedral for burial.
Royal yacht
A decree by the Ministry of the Navy of 18 May 1900 outlined the technical situation of the Spanish Navy's ships and directed the decommissioning of 25 ships deemed ineffective.

Giralda, due to its good condition and performance, although without any military value, and deficient in several respects as a dispatch vessel, is also useful for peacekeeping missions and international services to which the Navy may be justly obligated.
Thus retained by the Spanish Navy, Giralda began service as Spain's royal yacht.

Her first voyage in this capacity began on 16 August 1900, when Queen Regent Maria Christina, her children King Alfonso XIII, Maria de las Mercedes, and Maria Teresa, and Prime Minister Francisco Silvela boarded Giralda at San Sebastián to begin a cruise along the northern and Galician coasts of Spain.

Maria Christina wanted to give the 14-year-old Alfonso XIII both his first experience of life at sea and direct exposure to the coastal communities of northern and northwestern Spain. Accompanied by the gunboat Vasco Núñez de Balboa and the aviso Urania, Giralda reached Bilbao on 16 August.

As the cruise continued, the royal family arrived at Gijón on 18 August, Avilés on 20 August, A Coruña on 22 August, Muros, Villagarcía de Arosa, Marín, and Vigo on 28 August, Ferrol on 1 September, and Santander on 8 September before returning to San Sebastián on 10 September.
Thereafter, such summer cruises by the royal family became commonplace, and a tour of duty aboard Giralda was considered a high honor for Spanish naval officers.
As a junior officer, Manuel de Mendívil y Oliva, who would become a noted writer and the colonial governor of Spanish Guinea, served aboard Giralda early in her service as the royal yacht.

In 1901, a squadron under Cámara's command consisting of Emperador Carlos V, Urania, Vasco Núñez de Balboa, the battleship Pelayo, the coastal defense ships Numancia and Vitoria, the protected cruiser Río de la Plata, the destroyers Audaz, Osado, and Proserpina, the torpedo boats Habana, Halcón, and Orión, the gunboat Temerario, and the corvette Nautilus (serving as a training ship) was on hand to greet the royal family when it visited Ferrol aboard Giralda.
